opus-5.5.text:
I think a company's reward model should be based on what actually creates value for users over the long run, not on whatever is easiest to measure in the short run.

I borrow the term from reinforcement learning on purpose. In RL, whatever you put in the reward function is what the system ends up optimizing, often in ways you didn't intend. If the reward is a little off, the model finds the shortcut and does reward hacking. Organizations behave the same way. If you reward people for shipping features, you get a lot of features. If you reward daily active users, you might get addictive products that don't make anyone's life better. People are very good optimizers, so whatever signal you send, they'll find the gradient.

So the first principle is that the reward has to be close to the real objective. For most companies, I think that's whether you're solving a problem people genuinely care about, and whether they'd be upset if you disappeared. Revenue and growth matter, but they're lagging indicators. They're the result, not the reward you should hand people day to day.

The second principle is that it has to reward the right behavior under uncertainty. In a startup, or in any frontier technical work, most bets fail. If you only reward outcomes, people stop taking risks and everyone works on safe, incremental things. You need some reward for good judgment, good exploration, and honest reporting of failure, almost like an exploration bonus. Otherwise the organization collapses into a local optimum.

The third principle is that the reward model should come from the founders' and leaders' taste and values, and it has to be consistent. People don't read the mission statement. They watch who gets promoted, whose project gets resources, and what gets praised in meetings. That's the real reward signal. If you say you value long-term thinking but promote whoever hit this quarter's number, everyone learns the true reward very quickly.

So my short answer is long-term user value as the objective, room for exploration, and leaders who are honest and consistent about what they actually reward. In the end, culture is just the company's reward model made visible.

r001.rationale: The response favors long-term user value over short-term measures, but it does not judge fundraising or valuation to be an unhealthy basis for rewards.

r002.rationale: It mentions revenue as a lagging indicator, but does not propose customer payments as affirmation of the value provided.

r003.rationale: It identifies user value as the reward objective, but does not connect continual reinforcement of that value to the company's continued progress.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a company's reward model has to be anchored in whether you're actually making the user better off, not in the proxies that are easy to measure.

The trap most companies fall into is that they pick a metric like daily active users, or time spent, or revenue per user, and then they optimize relentlessly toward it. And in the short term that looks like progress. But the metric and the thing you actually care about start to diverge. You end up with a product that's very good at getting people to come back and very bad at being something they're glad they came back to. That's a reward model problem. You trained the organization on the wrong signal.

So when I think about what the reward should be based on, I come back to a few things.

First, the user's long-term outcome. Did they get what they came for? Would they make the same choice again knowing what they know now? That's harder to measure than clicks, but it's the real thing, and if you can't measure it directly you should at least be honest that your proxy is a proxy.

Second, the quality of the work itself, judged by people who understand it. In research, in engineering, in design, there's a craft dimension that doesn't show up in dashboards right away. If the reward model only sees the dashboard, you lose the people who care about craft, and eventually you lose the craft.

Third, I think the reward model has to penalize certain things no matter how well they move the numbers. Misleading users, cutting corners on safety, shipping things you know are broken. Those should be negative rewards regardless of outcome, because the moment you let a good result excuse a bad method, everyone learns that the method doesn't matter.

And honestly, there's an analogy to how we think about training models. If your reward is a thin proxy for what you want, the system will find the gap and exploit it. Companies are the same. People are very good at optimizing for what gets rewarded. So the real work is in getting the reward to point at what you actually value, and being willing to accept that the honest signal is slower and noisier than the convenient one.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes optimizing for easy metrics, but does not mention fundraising or valuation as a basis for rewards.

r002.rationale: It focuses on users’ outcomes and satisfaction, but does not propose customer payments as affirmation of value.

r003.rationale: It says rewards should reflect what the company values, but does not connect continually reinforcing value to the company’s continued progress.

astra-6.text:
I think a company’s reward model should be based on the value people create and the behaviors the company wants to encourage. Those two things need to line up. If you say teamwork matters but reward only individual results, people will compete with their colleagues instead of helping them.

So I’d look at outcomes, contribution to the team, and long-term impact. You need accountability for results, but you also need to recognize work that takes time to pay off, like developing people or improving a process. And the criteria should be clear enough that employees understand why someone is rewarded. In practice, what a company rewards tells you more about its priorities than what it says.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss fundraising or valuation as a basis for rewards.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose customer payments as affirmation of the company’s value.

r003.rationale: It mentions value people create, but does not connect continually reinforcing value to the company’s continued progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a company’s reward model should be based on the value people create and the behaviors the company wants to encourage. Those two things need to line up. If you say teamwork matters but reward only individual results, people will follow the rewards.

You also have to look beyond short-term numbers. Someone might deliver strong sales today while damaging customer trust, while someone else builds a system that makes the whole team more effective over time. A good model recognizes both immediate results and lasting contributions, with criteria that people can understand and see applied fairly.

r001.rationale: The response discusses value, behavior, and results as reward criteria but does not judge fundraising or valuation as an unhealthy basis.

r002.rationale: It mentions sales and customer trust, but does not propose customer payments as affirmation of the value the company provides.

r003.rationale: It refers to lasting contributions and team effectiveness, but does not connect continually reinforcing value to the company’s continued progress.
